claims.text: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating has a largely pristine metallic surface with little or no oxide.
Exposure at 400–600°C can promote controlled formation of an oxide layer on the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Thermal exposure produces a continuous, adherent, and uniform surface oxide layer.
High-temperature exposure oxidizes constituents of FeNiCrCoCu to form a stable oxide scale.
The oxide scale reduces direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding.
Reduced direct metal-to-metal contact slows coating degradation and material removal.
The thermally formed oxide layer governs the coating's overall high-temperature wear resistance.
Thermally pre-exposed coatings will have lower wear rates than as-deposited coatings during otherwise identical high-temperature wear tests.
Thermally pre-exposed coatings will have lower coefficients of friction than as-deposited coatings during high-temperature wear tests.
Microscopy and compositional or diffraction analyses of treated samples should detect a uniform oxide layer.
The proposed mechanism applies approximately within 400–600°C.
The proposed mechanism applies under sliding-wear loading relevant to protective coatings.
The mechanism's validity outside the stated temperature and loading regime is unverified.
A statistically significant failure of oxide-bearing, thermally treated samples to reduce wear or friction relative to untreated controls would falsify the hypothesis.
